verification_notes: BIGGEST CORRECTION - the 2018 data gap is only half-closed. CAG Appendices 3.5-3.7 do give 112 daily rows each, 10-06-2018 to 29-09-2018 (confirmed by date-sorted extraction, not string sort), but they are SIMULATION tables. Cross-diffing Appendix 3.5 (1983 curve) against 3.6 (2020 curve) proves it: identical inflow, divergent level and spill. What AquaSync actually gains is a genuine daily 2018 INFLOW series for Idukki and Idamalayar plus observed powerhouse discharge on the flood days - still a real closure of gap 1 - but NOT an observed level or spill record. Observed spills exist only as 5-day aggregates in Tables 3.6/3.7/3.8 (Idukki 467.51 MCM, Idamalayar 340.50 MCM), and daily observed Neeleswaram flow in Table 3.4.

THE RULE CURVE IS NOT INTERPOLATED, AND THIS MATTERS OPERATIONALLY. CAG Appendix 3.3 gives the 2020 curve at 18 ten-day steps and I verified all 36 values. The KSDMA bulletin of 25 Aug 2026 lists Idukki rule level 2390.09 ft = 728.4994 m, which is exactly the 31 August row - not the linear interpolation between 20 Aug (727.50) and 31 Aug (728.50), which would give 727.955 m. KSEB therefore appears to apply the curve as a step function holding the end-of-period value. An optimiser that linearly interpolates the published curve will silently target a level about 0.5 m below what KSEB is actually holding to in late August.

THE CENTRAL COMPLICATION SURVIVES SCRUTINY AND IS CORRECTLY STATED. I read Tables 3.6, 3.7 and 3.8 directly. Idukki actual spills 14-18 Aug 467.51 MCM; 1983 curve 558.19; 2020 curve 531.03; only the 1983 curve initialised from the LOWER rule level gives 308.13 MCM. Idamalayar 2020 curve 323.49 vs 340.50 actual (5% better). The 2020 rule curve KSEB actually adopted would have made Idukki worse. Any AquaSync narrative that frames rule-curve compliance as the fix is contradicted by the official audit.

THE FORECAST-SKILL FLOOR CLAIM IS THE STRONGEST FINDING IN THE SWEEP AND IT IS VERBATIM CORRECT. Current Science 116(5) p.789: 'The probability of detection (POD) of higher rainfall (>25 mm/day) at short range (3-day) or medium range (5-day) even with the ensemble of models is still low at about 20% to 30% only with a large probability of false alarm.' Set against Lake Mendocino's verified CNRFC numbers (24-hr inflow R2 0.84 at day 1 falling to 0.53 at day 5), the gap between the Periyar and the FIRO flagship sites is stark. Citation caveat: Sudheer et al. are citing their own references 23 and 24 here, not reporting an original result.

FIVE 403s WERE GENUINE BOT BLOCKING, NOT DEAD LINKS, AND ALL FIVE RESOURCES ARE REAL - but note one important asymmetry. ascelibrary (Das et al.), Wiley/agupubs (Delaney, Brodeur, Albano, Forbis & Ly) and gao.gov all block automated agents; every one was confirmed via Crossref, OpenAlex, DOAJ or WebFetch. Delaney, Brodeur, Albano and Forbis & Ly are all open access (CC BY or CC BY-NC) and readable in a browser. Das et al. 2025 is genuinely CLOSED (OpenAlex is_oa = false, no green copy anywhere) - and it is the paper closest to AquaSync's own thesis.

Albano et al.: 0. THE STRONGEST ACTIONABLE FINDING IS THE CHEAPEST TO IMPLEMENT, AND IT IS NOT ABOUT FORECASTS. Koo et al., verified verbatim: 'optimisation methodologies have not been widely applied in real-time operation due to disparities between research assumptions and practical requirements. To address this gap, we include practical objectives, such as minimising the magnitude and frequency of changes in the existing outflow schedule.' Combined with Dam Safety Act s.41/s.42 (verified word for word - one year imprisonment for refusing a direction, two if it causes loss of life, head of department deemed guilty) and Rayner et al., the picture is consistent: an optimiser that proposes large or frequent deviations from the published schedule will not be adopted regardless of how good its foresight is. Adding a deviation-magnitude and deviation-frequency penalty to AquaSync's objective has more adoption value than any accuracy gain.

AN UNEXPECTED LEAD ON THE PRE-2020 DATA GAP, found while checking a different claim. The Google Flood Forecasting page itself points to the Google Runoff Reanalysis & Reforecast dataset (GRRR), described as global river discharge estimates covering 1980-2023, and an Inundation History dataset covering 1999-2020 - both separate from the waitlisted forecast API and neither in the source list. Given that AquaSync has no genuine pre-2020 Periyar operational data and CAG only supplies Jun-Sep 2018 inflow, a global discharge reanalysis back to 1980 is worth a dedicated look. I have NOT verified GRRR's resolution, Periyar coverage or access terms - flagging it as a lead, not a confirmed source.
